description: Six Information Systems Engineering students from Sonora, Mexico. Like desert owls, we thrive in the dark: turning complex NASA data into clear, powerful tools through full-stack development, data engineering and design.
summary:
Kairos is an interactive web tool that helps mission planners, educators and the public choose where and when to land at the Moon’s south pole. At the pole, the Sun and Earth hover just a few degrees above the horizon, so a single ridge can cut off solar power or direct-to-Earth communication. In 2024, the Odysseus lander touched down near the pole on a steep slope and tipped over: the wrong place, at the wrong time.

Kairos lets users “stand” at any site on a 3D lunar globe and watch the Sun and Earth move against the real terrain horizon. It compares the nine Artemis III candidate regions, notable missions, or any custom coordinate side by side, showing sunlit hours, Earth-visibility windows, and live countdowns to sunset and Earthset. It also plans a full mission timeline and finds the safest flat spot within a region using LOLA slope data.

Built on NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides and LRO/LOLA terrain, Kairos turns complex, expert-only tools into a clear visual answer: the right place, at the right time.
details:
What it does. Kairos is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. Users pick one of the nine Artemis III south-pole candidate regions, a notable mission site (Apollo 11, Chang’e 4, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, IM-1) or any custom latitude/longitude, then choose a date. Kairos places them on the surface in 3D and shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real terrain horizon. It reports solar elevation, total sunlit hours, direct-to-Earth visibility windows, and live countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset. A comparison view puts sites side by side, a mission planner lays out the whole surface stay, and a slope check uses LOLA terrain to find the safest flat spot within a region.

How it works. A Python pipeline queries NASA JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions as seen from each site, builds a local horizon profile from LRO/LOLA elevation data, and computes when each body is above or below the terrain. The results are exported as JSON that the front end reads.

Benefits and impact. Existing ephemeris tools are powerful but built for experts. Kairos turns the same data into a visual answer that mission planners, educators and the public can read in seconds. It makes power and communication constraints visible before a mission commits to a site. Odysseus (2024) landed on a steep slope near the pole and tipped over, which shows how costly a poor choice of place and time can be.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite and Tailwind CSS for the web app, with a WebGL 3D globe. Python for the data pipeline. Data from NASA JPL Horizons, LRO/LOLA, LROC QuickMap and NASA Moon Trek. GitHub for collaboration. Claude was used as an AI assistant for code and content.

Creativity. Instead of tables of angles, Kairos lets you “stand” on the Moon and watch the Sun and Earth sink behind real ridges. The line to each body turns dashed when it is blocked. Energy and communication are judged together, on one timeline.

Factors considered. Accuracy, using official NASA ephemerides and terrain. Usability for non-experts. The low Sun and Earth angles at the pole, where a few degrees of terrain decide everything. Slope safety. Support for any site, not only Artemis. Full citation of NASA data sources.
